transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-22
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (ByteWave CTO), Lina Park (ByteWave ML Engineer), Jordan Lee (ByteWave Infra)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood inference, joined by priya on the technical side, we'll run through optimize and specifically quant profiles int8 and fp8 and then show a few benchmarks, um if you have Qs interrupt anytime
[00:20] Priya: hi all, hey sam, lina, jordan, quick agenda: why quant profiles matter, demo in console, tradeoffs quality vs latency, and then next steps for a poc
[00:37] Sam: cool, yeah we are really focused on reducing token cost for our summarization pipeline but without regressing on quality, timeline is tight - hoping to start pilot in the next 2 weeks
[00:50] Lina: and we run variable sequence lengths, 64 to 2k tokens, lots of short queries and some long sessions so latency spike matters
[01:10] Priya: got it, that's actually a typical pattern where batching and kv-cache behavior changes on longer sequences, we'll highlight that. quick q: are you currently using any quantized models in prod?
[01:25] Sam: no, currently running FP16 on dedicated inference nodes via our cloud provider, we've looked at triton but haven't committed. cost is climbing
[01:40] Alex: great context. one thing to flag: in our optimize toolkit we recommend profiling your workload to pick a quant profile — int8 typically gives best cost reduction, fp8 tends to hit a sweet spot on certain LLMs for quality but with slightly higher runtime
[02:05] Priya: jumping into console — (screen share notes) so here's the optimize tab, you can upload a small eval set, choose quality metrics, and then run candidate quant profiles. note: our UI sometimes labels fp8 as 'FP8 (experimental)' depending on model family, cause folks are testing different kernels
[02:35] [03:00] Priya: here's an example run we did for a 13B model: baseline fp16 latency 120ms p95, int8 reduced token cost by ~45% and p95 latency down to ~85ms, fp8 quality delta was ~1.5% on ROUGE but latency was about 95ms. these numbers obviously vary with hardware and sequence distribution
[03:40] Lina: that 1.5% is in rouge, how about human eval?
[03:50] Priya: good q — in our lab human eval showed very small perceived difference for summarization tasks between fp16 and fp8, int8 sometimes had more diffs on instruction-following prompts depending on quant scheme
[04:10] Sam: what about safety filters? do these quant changes affect safety classifiers or rerankers?
[04:20] Alex: we recommend keeping safety/filters at higher precision or as a hosted service. you can mix and match — serve generation on quantized model and run safety checks on FP16/FP32 endpoints
[04:40] [05:05] Priya: also the KV cache can amplify latency regressions on long contexts if kernel selection isn't optimized, our runtime will pick different kernels, and optimize suggests a quant profile per model + sequence length bucket to avoid surprises
[05:35] Jordan: we run large throughput, what's the impact on GPU memory with int8 vs fp8?
[05:45] Priya: memory footprint drops with int8 more than fp8 — roughly 2x reduction vs fp16 for int8 in many cases; fp8 is between int8 and fp16. but kernel support and memory alignment can cause small variations
[06:10] Alex: one caveat — for some models we saw higher decoding latency with int8 for short sequences because of extra dequantize steps; that's where batching and our automatic batching config helps
[06:30] [07:00] Priya: demo: uploading a 200-sample eval set, metric = ROUGE-l and a small human-score proxy. running profile: baseline fp16 -> int8 -> fp8
[07:20] Priya: results populating, ok baseline perf + quality table, notice the quality delta column, int8 shows -2.3% on this sample, fp8 shows -0.8%. latency p95 numbers attached
[07:45] Lina: those deltas are non-trivial for us; we need guardrails if we go int8
[07:55] Alex: totally, and that's why Optimize can save per-prompt thresholds and set an automatic rollback to fallback model variants if quality drops below a threshold in production
[08:20] [09:00] Sam: curious about model compatibility — do you support both open models and redwood-verified ones? we use an open 13b family
[09:10] Priya: yes we support many open families; for each we provide recommended quant profiles and kernels. sometimes fp8 kernels are vendor-specific and we call out compatibility (e.g., ampere vs hopper differences)
[09:35] Jordan: do you have P95 numbers for both hosted and dedicated? we might want to compare dedicated reserved capacity vs hosted API
[09:45] Alex: yes, we attach mode-by-mode benchmarks. typically dedicated with pinned GPUs has slightly lower jitter and can be tuned for latency; hosted route is simpler to start and you get automatic fallback routing. we'll include both in the spreadsheet
[10:10] [11:00] Priya: here's an illustration — heatmap of quality vs latency across sequence length buckets. notice int8 shines for short tokens in throughput scenarios, but for 1k+ sequences fp8 sometimes preserves quality better while not doubling latency
[11:30] Lina: can optimize do per-route quant profiles? like production vs staging?
[11:40] Alex: yup, per-route and per-model version. you can assign policies: route X uses fp8, route Y uses int8 for cheaper queries, and fallback to fp16 on errors or quality regression
[12:00] [13:00] Priya: quick note on infrastructure: we integrate with KMS/HSM for keys, audit logs included, and there's RBAC in the console. customers with strict compliance often pick dedicated or private deployment
[13:20] Sam: we need SOC2 and encryption at rest details — we'll take the deck but high level please confirm it exists
[13:30] Alex: yes SOC2 and KMS details in the security deck, will send link after call
[13:45] [15:00] Priya: back to the bench, one subtlety — quant-aware distillation and linting of tokenization can move quality closer to baseline, but it's extra work. for a quick win we recommend fp8 on the first pass and measure, then try int8 with a focused eval set
[15:30] Lina: do you have automated A/B testing to flag quality regressions in production?
[15:40] Alex: yes, rollout policies in console can run A/B or canary with automatic rollback. quality monitoring ties to eval sets and prompt-level thresholds
[16:05] Jordan: what about throughput scheduling and batching knobs? we have bursty traffic patterns
[16:15] Priya: autoscaling + continuous batching helps; our smart batching groups similar-length requests and will prefer hot-key caching for prefixes. note: batching increases latency for single requests but improves cost per token for high throughput
[16:45] [18:00] Priya: demo: configuring a rollout policy — create route, attach quant profile, set canary 10% traffic, and set quality threshold 0.5% ROUGE drop allowed
[18:30] Sam: if canary fails does traffic revert automatically?
[18:35] Alex: yes, automatic fallback to previous model/version or to fp16 baseline depending on policy
[19:00] Lina: few more specifics — our dataset has domain-specific tokens, will quantization blow up on out-of-vocab tokens?
[19:15] Priya: quant affects weights not tokenization; but quantization can increase hallucination in corner cases — hence the eval set should include your domain prompts. sometimes we recommend per-token biases or ngram blockers
[19:45] [21:00] Sam: ok realistic ask — can you run a baseline POC with our 500 sample eval set and provide both fp8 and int8 configs with latency and quality tables?
[21:15] Alex: yes we can. typical POC includes three runs: baseline fp16, fp8, int8. we'll return a spreadsheet with ROUGE, human-proxy, p50/p95 latency, and cost delta.
[21:40] Jordan: how long will that take? we need quick iteration
[21:50] Priya: if you share the eval and a small sample dataset today, we can run initial bench in 48-72 hours depending on queue. for production-like runs we'll schedule dedicated capacity which takes longer to provision
[22:10] [23:00] Alex: other implementation notes — you can also use our SDK to run offline quant profile simulations if you prefer to test in your infra before POC. we'll share examples
[23:30] Lina: any known models where int8 is a no-go?
[23:40] Priya: some early decoder-only variants with nonstandard attention patterns have poor int8 support; we flag those in the model catalog. often fp8 is safer as a middle-ground
[24:00] Sam: competitors — we're also talking to openai and anthro which offer managed endpoints, any guidance on how redwood compares?
[24:10] Alex: high level: Redwood focuses on production economics and flexibility — you get more knobs (quant profiles, per-route policies, dedicated/private) and visibility into cost breakdowns. managed vendors are simpler but less flexible on custom quant/kernel choices
[24:40] [26:00] Priya: demo: attaching the quant benchmark spreadsheet (we shared a link) — sample rows show model, sequence bucket, metric delta, latency p95, cost delta
[26:30] Lina: looks good. can you annotate rows where fp8 is recommended vs int8?
[26:40] Priya: yes we'll add a recommended column and confidence score based on our lab runs
[27:00] Sam: security again — will POC data leave our VPC? we prefer private deployment for sensitive data
[27:10] Alex: for POC we can run in dedicated or private depending on contract. hosted POC can be done with strict retention and SOC2+KMS, but if you need network isolation we can spin a private instance
[27:40] Jordan: cost implication? private > dedicated > hosted typically?
[27:50] Alex: roughly yes; private has higher infra/setup cost but best for compliance. dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower unit cost at scale, hosted is quickest to start
[28:10] [30:00] Priya: final demo snippet — threshold-based rollback in action (we simulate higher ROUGE drop and show automatic fallback to fp16), small bit of lag due to screen share
[30:30] Lina: ok that gives confidence. next steps?
[30:40] Alex: recap: Alex will send the quant benchmark spreadsheet + pricing + security deck by 2026-05-24; Priya will prep POC run templates and configs by 2026-05-25; ByteWave (Jordan) to provide eval dataset by 2026-05-26. we'll tentatively schedule the POC kickoff 2026-05-28
[31:10] Sam: sounds good, thanks both.
[31:20] Alex: thanks everyone, any last qs?
[31:30] Lina: none from me
[31:40] Jordan: no, thanks
[31:50] Alex: we'll follow up in email with links. bye
[32:00] call ended

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts ("K V cash" instead of KV cache, "Opti-mise" spelled differently), speaker labels approximate.
